blocks.text: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals in Iowa despite concerns
The US military is set to deonate 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500lb of lead azide in Iowa at 10am Eastern time on Wednesday.
As the Guardian has previously reported, the army has changed the date three times after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa, where the plant is situated. The army has warned that the blast could release a plume of toxic lead dust extending up to 100 miles northeast, possibly reaching cities such as Wapello and New Boston, Illinois.
Last week, Iowa governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican, activated the state emergency management office, and the state created a website for information about the detonation.

blocks.text: Iowa braces for blast that could spread lead plume over 100-mile radius

The US Army is set to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

The controlled blast is planned to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes.
On Tuesday, the army released new maps forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri.

The army has warned that “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

The detonation is currently scheduled for 10am ET. In a public safety advisory released on Tuesday, the army said: “A more precise time will be communicated after evaluating changing weather patterns and waiting for the safest possible conditions.”
My colleague Cecilia Nowell has more here:
US army map shows projected path of toxic dust from Iowa detonation
Edward Helmore
The US army has released new maps showing the projected path of a toxic lead dust plume from the planned detonation of 68 barrels – five tons – of lead axide at an Iowa ammunition dump.
Projections show a plume moving south-west of the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, stretching through a south-eastern portion of the state before extending into northern Missouri.

The army sent an emergency notification to cellphones on Tuesday confirming the time of the controlled explosion – and warning that some people within five miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated.
The “imminent threat alert” told those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”.

The army said it had set up additional “blast barriers” around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated. It also said it would apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust and douse the explosive materials with thousands of gallons of water.

Acting secretary of the army Adam Telle said in a post on X that there was no reason for the public to panic. He said it was “unanimous judgment” of various government entities that the army “should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation”.
